meta.title: Who really said "When I'm good, I'm very good. But when I'm bad, I'm better"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Mae West wrote and spoke it. The line is her own dialogue from the 1933 Paramount film I'm No Angel, delivered as Tira to Cary Grant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When I'm good, I'm very good. But when I'm bad, I'm better'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Mae West: she wrote it herself for I'm No Angel (1933) and delivered it as Tira to Cary Grant. A verified line, not a fabricated quip.

answer.label: Written & spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Mae West wrote this line herself — she received sole story, screenplay and all-dialogue credit on I’m No Angel (1933) — and delivered it on screen as the character Tira. The popular wording (“When I’m good, I’m very good. But when I’m bad, I’m better”) matches the film dialogue almost exactly.

source.excerpt: Well, when I’m good — I’m very good. But, when I’m bad — I’m better.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced Mae West quotes, attributed to I’m No Angel (1933).
Wikipedia confirms West received sole story, screenplay and all-dialogue credit on the film, playing the character Tira.
A scene reading by a Cary Grant film blog places the line in the romantic exchange with Grant and notes West’s trademark delivery.
source.excerptNote: Delivered in a romantic scene with Cary Grant — ostensibly about her nerve as a lion-tamer, but plainly about something else entirely.

source.rightsHolder: Paramount Pictures (film) and the Estate of Mae West (screenplay)
source.rightsNote: The line is dialogue from I’m No Angel, first released by Paramount Pictures in 1933 — a work published well after the U.S. public-domain cutoff, so it remains in copyright. Rights sit with the studio holding the film (Paramount’s pre-1950 sound features are now controlled by Universal) and with Mae West’s estate as author of the screenplay.

author.name: Mae West
author.heading: About Mae West
author.bio: Mae West (1893–1980) was an American vaudeville star, Broadway playwright and Hollywood actress famous for her double-entendre wit and self-authored material. She wrote her own plays (including the notorious 1926 production Sex) and, at Paramount in the early 1930s, wrote or heavily shaped the dialogue for her own films — making her one of the rare stars of the era who effectively scripted her most-quoted lines.

misattribution.heading: Wording & the “spontaneous quip” myth
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Mae West is correct — the caveats are about wording and origin, not authorship.

items.why: A frequently-circulated variant reads “When I’m good I’m very, very good…” (see this doubled-‘very’ version). The film line uses a single “very good.”

It is often passed around as one of West’s off-the-cuff real-life witticisms. In fact it is scripted dialogue she wrote herself for a specific film role — arguably a stronger claim to authorship, not a weaker one.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: really Mae West, and really her own words — written for and spoken in I’m No Angel (1933).

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The line distills West’s whole screen persona into a single breath: unbothered, in command, and franker about desire than the incoming Production Code would soon allow. Because she authored her own dialogue, it reads as autobiography as much as script.
